edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and consequential continuing stories with fresh reporting. Returning coverage is included only where there is a material new development, including the Rosebank decision outlook and the latest PHP security response.

content.headline: Missile attack on Kyiv follows new push to resume Ukraine peace talks
content.shortHeadline: Kyiv hit as Russia says it is ready to resume peace talks
content.standfirst: Six people were injured in an attack on the Ukrainian capital hours after Russia signalled willingness to restart talks. The proposals remain unclear, and Moscow has dismissed ideas from Kyiv and its European partners as lacking substance.

image.caption: Russian missile and drone attacks have hit Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

sources.originalTitle: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
Ukraine war briefing: New peace proposals lack ‘substance’, says Kremlin after Witkoff-Putin meeting in Russia
Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
USA og Rusland taler fred og forretning: 'Ukraine risikerer at betale prisen'

segments.body: Missiles struck Kyiv overnight, damaging homes and injuring six people, the city’s mayor said. The attack came hours after Russia said it was ready in principle to resume peace talks and US President Donald Trump said he believed an end to the war was closer than before.

segments.title: Talks, but no clear breakthrough
segments.body: US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg after talks with Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders in Oslo. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Russia could resume talks at a technical level around mid-November, but described the proposals from Kyiv and Europe as having little substance. Zelensky has said Ukraine could accept a freeze along the current front line, with security guarantees still to be discussed.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s Russia editor argues that Putin has shown little desire to meet Zelensky and may not feel pressure to end the war, given Ukraine’s strained air defences and the prospect of closer US-Russia ties.

segments.body: A separate concern is that diplomacy could become entangled with economic deals. A Danish analyst quoted by DR warns that closer US-Russia ties and a push for a rapid settlement could leave Ukraine facing pressure to make major concessions, while investment in occupied territory could help entrench Russian control.

perspectives.body: DIIS researcher Flemming Splidsboel Hansen says a ceasefire is not necessarily a good peace: the terms must also be acceptable to Ukraine and its European partners.

content.headline: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
content.shortHeadline: US orders diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
content.standfirst: Three people were killed in attacks at an airport and an oil facility, according to Saudi authorities. Washington ordered non-emergency staff and their families to leave, warning that hostilities could escalate rapidly.

image.caption: Smoke rises near Taiz, Yemen, during fighting involving Houthi forces.

sources.originalTitle: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
Some US diplomats told to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks

segments.body: The US State Department has ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks intensify. Saudi authorities said a strike at King Fahd International Airport killed one person and injured eight; falling debris from an intercepted drone near an oil field killed two more.

segments.title: Reports of wider withdrawals disputed
segments.body: The State Department cited attacks by Iran-backed Houthis on civilian infrastructure. Reports said US families were also being withdrawn from other Gulf countries, but a department spokesperson described those reports as inaccurate and said the order applied only to Saudi Arabia. Neither attack was immediately claimed by the Houthis.

content.headline: Vance defends Ohio attack ad that uses rival’s family history
content.shortHeadline: Vance tells Republicans to stop complaining about Ohio attack ad
content.standfirst: The ad features the estranged mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton, whose stepfather was charged with sexually abusing her as a child. Ramaswamy’s campaign has claimed responsibility and plans to spend millions airing it.

image.caption: Democratic Ohio governor candidate Amy Acton greets voters at a parade in Cleveland.

sources.originalTitle: Vance tells Republicans to 'stop whining' about controversial Ohio attack ad
Mor angriber sin egen datter i valgreklame - Vance beder partifæller 'stoppe med at klynke'

segments.body: US Vice-President JD Vance told Republicans to stop “whining” about an attack ad targeting Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor. The ad features Acton’s mother calling her a liar, but does not mention that Acton and her brother were removed from their mother’s custody after their stepfather was charged with raping Acton as a child.

segments.title: Backlash across party lines
segments.body: Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign has confirmed it made the ad and pledged to spend $4m airing it. Republicans and Democrats have criticised it, including Acton’s brother, who says the campaign has turned alleged abuse into a political talking point. The stepfather was never prosecuted and died in 2004.

The race is considered competitive, and a political analyst cited by the BBC said the ad could backfire by discouraging voters from supporting Ramaswamy. That remains a prediction, not an established effect of the campaign.

content.headline: New Mexico judge orders Meta to pay $25bn over user data claims
content.shortHeadline: Meta ordered to pay $25bn in New Mexico privacy case
content.standfirst: A judge found that Facebook’s owner repeatedly misled the public about user data and other practices. Meta says it will appeal, so the ruling may not be the final word in the case.

image.caption: Meta has faced a series of legal cases and penalties.

sources.originalTitle: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy

segments.body: A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25bn after a jury found the company violated state laws by misleading the public about how Facebook user data was handled and shared. The judge said the alleged misrepresentations were deliberate and continued for more than 11 years.

segments.title: Meta plans an appeal
segments.body: The state had sought up to $40bn in penalties; the judge reduced a calculated total of $219bn to $25bn. Meta’s lawyer called the ruling an obstacle to doing business in New Mexico and said the company intends to appeal. The lawsuit also concerned claims about how Meta handled content including hate speech.

content.headline: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots with false claims
content.shortHeadline: Macron says foreign leaders exploited French riots with false claims
content.standfirst: The French president accused unnamed leaders of using the unrest for electoral gain, after Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu blamed it on immigration. Macron said there was no visible foreign interference in the riots themselves.

image.caption: Protesters rally in Lille during demonstrations across France.

sources.originalTitle: Macron accuses foreign leaders of exploiting French riots
Katya Adler: France divided over who to blame for riots and what to learn from them

segments.body: Emmanuel Macron accused foreign leaders of exploiting recent riots in France for election campaigning, apparently referring to Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu. He said claims that France had been “invaded” by migrants and Islamists were false, and that foreign manipulation of information had followed the violence.

segments.title: False material circulates online
segments.body: The report describes AI-generated videos and images shared as if they showed real events. One widely viewed image of an elderly couple allegedly robbed in Paris was created with ChatGPT, its maker told the BBC; the claim it illustrated remains unconfirmed. Macron said the leaders’ comments had been influenced by fake videos.

The French government has blamed far-left groups for much of the unrest, while people involved in student protests have rejected claims that politicians directed them. Macron said there was no visible foreign interference in the events themselves. Reports of online amplification by foreign-linked accounts remain attributed to security officials and researchers.

content.headline: Arab voters could shape Israel’s election, but coalition options remain limited
content.shortHeadline: Arab voter turnout could shape Israel’s close election
content.standfirst: Arab citizens make up about a fifth of Israel’s population, and their parties may hold seats needed to form a government. Yet several opposition leaders have ruled out working with them before the vote.

image.caption: Arabic election posters become more common on the approach to Umm al-Fahm in northern Israel.

sources.originalTitle: De udgør en femtedel af Israels befolkning – deres stemmer kan blive afgørende for landets fremtid
The simple way Netanyahu’s reign could be ended by Israel’s opposition
Tidligere generalstabschef udfordrer Netanyahu

segments.body: As Israel approaches election day, Arab citizens’ turnout could affect which bloc can form a government. In 2022, about 60% of voters in Umm al-Fahm did not vote; some residents interviewed by DR say they intend to take part this time and want a government without far-right ministers.

segments.title: Votes do not guarantee influence
segments.body: Polling cited by DR suggests Arab parties could win enough seats to matter in a closely divided parliament. But opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has said he will not form an alliance with Arab parties, while other opposition figures have also ruled out such a coalition. The parties themselves differ on what support they would offer.

perspectives.body: Residents interviewed in Umm al-Fahm and Nazareth describe both national concerns and local priorities, including violence and crime, equality and the future of their communities.

content.headline: Germany’s AfD proposes sweeping overhaul of EU institutions
content.shortHeadline: AfD plan would abolish EU Parliament and cut the bloc’s powers
content.standfirst: The party says it wants to stay in the EU while radically reducing its authority, including by replacing the elected parliament with national delegations. Critics warn the proposal would weaken democratic representation.

image.caption: AfD co-leader Alice Weidel, pictured in an archive photograph.

sources.originalTitle: AfD fremlægger vision for EU: Vil nedlægge EU-Parlamentet og begrænse budget

segments.body: Alternative for Germany co-leader Alice Weidel has presented a plan to reshape the EU from within rather than leave it. It proposes renegotiating the bloc’s treaties, cutting its institutions and budget, and replacing the European Parliament with delegations appointed by national governments.

segments.title: Critics warn of a democratic retreat
segments.body: The plan would also reduce the European Commission to an administrative role and replace the EU Court of Justice with an arbitration body. European Parliament vice-president Christel Schaldemose called it an attack on European democracy, arguing that voters should retain the right to elect their representatives.

content.headline: Pope Leo will need no further cancer treatment after surgery, doctors say
content.shortHeadline: Pope Leo needs no further cancer treatment, doctors say
content.standfirst: Doctors say tests found the illness limited to the local area after surgery to remove part of the Pope’s right lung. Whether he will make a planned trip to South America in November is still unclear.

image.caption: Pope Leo returns to St Peter’s Square for his weekly audience after surgery.

sources.originalTitle: Paven skal ikke have yderligere kræftbehandling efter operation

segments.body: Pope Leo will not need further treatment after surgery for lung cancer, according to his doctors. They said tests confirmed the diagnosis but found the disease was limited to the local area. The 71-year-old had part of his right lung removed on 13 October and has begun returning to his usual duties.

The Vatican has not said whether the Pope will make a planned visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from 6 to 17 November. He was discharged from hospital on Saturday and returned to St Peter’s Square on Wednesday for his weekly audience.

content.headline: PHP security flaw prompts global website shutdowns and urgent patching
content.shortHeadline: PHP security flaw prompts urgent patching and website shutdowns
content.standfirst: Governments and cyber agencies are warning organisations to update a widely used web programming language or take vulnerable systems offline. Experts say the public disclosure may leave a long tail of sites exposed to attack.

image.caption: A security patch is available for the PHP flaw, but vulnerable websites still need to apply it.

sources.originalTitle: Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
Flaw in PHP computer language leads to shutdown of websites around world

segments.body: Websites and public services have been taken offline as organisations respond to two serious vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used across the web. A fix has been issued, and the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre has urged organisations to patch systems or consider taking them offline until they are protected.

segments.title: A race to find and fix vulnerable systems
segments.body: The flaws had remained hidden for more than a decade. Security researchers warn that attackers may now try to exploit them, while organisations may not know every place PHP is running in their systems. The NCSC also advises checking for signs that an attacker may already have gained access.

Websites associated with several UK councils and BBC programmes were reported offline, but the BBC had not confirmed that all the outages were linked to PHP. The vulnerability’s full reach is not yet known, and the PHP Foundation’s update is available only for newer versions; users of older versions are urged to upgrade.

content.headline: Rosebank oilfield rejection reportedly under consideration after Jackdaw gas nod
content.shortHeadline: Energy secretary reportedly leaning against Rosebank oilfield
content.standfirst: Officials say Miatta Fahnbulleh is minded to reject the major oilfield, but no decision has been made and the prime minister could still be involved. The contrast with Wednesday’s approval of Jackdaw has sharpened a political and climate debate.

image.caption: Offshore workers arrive at Aberdeen airport after a shift in the North Sea.

sources.originalTitle: Energy secretary leaning towards rejecting Rosebank oilfield
UK approves Jackdaw gasfield in North Sea
North Sea drilling has been approved – here’s what it means for your energy bills
Climate campaigners condemn ‘maddening’ decision to approve Jackdaw gasfield
‘Jackdaw means we pay our mortgages’: relief in Aberdeen over gasfield approval

segments.body: The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is reportedly leaning towards rejecting the Rosebank oilfield, though officials say she has not made a final decision. The Guardian reports that Prime Minister Andy Burnham could have the final say if there is disagreement. A decision is expected before the end of the year.

segments.title: A distinction between gas and oil
segments.body: Fahnbulleh has argued that Jackdaw, which will produce gas for the domestic market, is different from Rosebank, whose oil is mainly for export. The government approved Jackdaw on Wednesday, saying it would support energy security and be compatible with climate commitments. Fahnbulleh has said it will not bring down household bills.

segments.title: Jobs and climate remain contested
segments.body: The Jackdaw decision has drawn criticism from climate campaigners, who argue it will add emissions without reducing bills or reversing the North Sea jobs decline. In Aberdeen, workers told the Guardian they hope the field will help sustain incomes in the short term, while acknowledging that it is unlikely to restore the city’s former boom years.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s Aberdeen reporting captures a local employment concern: offshore workers say renewables have not yet replaced the region’s oil and gas jobs, even as some businesses are shifting towards wind power.

content.headline: MPs warn Royal Navy lacks ships and submarines to deter Russia in the High North
content.shortHeadline: MPs warn Royal Navy is short of ships and submarines for Russia threat
content.standfirst: A parliamentary committee says gaps in frigates, destroyers and attack submarines risk undermining the UK’s ability to respond to Russian activity beyond Scotland. It wants a plan to put more vessels at sea by 2030.

image.caption: The destroyer HMS Dragon took more than three weeks to reach the eastern Mediterranean after a drone strike on a UK base in Cyprus.

sources.originalTitle: Royal Navy lacks resources to counter Russian threat in high north, MPs warn

segments.body: The Commons defence select committee says the Royal Navy lacks the available warships and submarines needed to operate effectively in the High North. Its report cites low availability of destroyers, frigates and attack submarines, and calls for “dramatic progress” before the end of the decade.

segments.title: Shortfalls and a reliance on allies
segments.body: The committee points to a shortage of frigates equipped to detect submarines and says all five Astute-class attack submarines were in dock for part of the summer. It warns that the UK would face critical military gaps if the US did not assist during a crisis involving a smaller NATO member in the region.

content.headline: Storm Austen brings an amber warning for south-west England
content.shortHeadline: Amber warning issued as Storm Austen hits south-west England
content.standfirst: The Met Office warns of a risk to life from strong winds and large waves in parts of Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly. Warnings may change as forecasters assess the storm’s track.

image.caption: The Met Office warns of dangerous waves and strong winds in parts of Cornwall and Devon.

sources.originalTitle: Why the UK could see a winter of floods – as first named storm of season arrives

segments.body: An amber weather warning is in force from Thursday evening for parts of south-west England, where gusts could exceed 70mph on exposed coasts. The Met Office warns of large waves and disruption until Friday afternoon, as the first named storm of the season, Austen, arrives.

segments.title: Stay clear of the water
segments.body: The RNLI has urged people not to take unnecessary risks near the coast and not to enter the water to help someone in difficulty. It advises calling the Coastguard, telling the person to float and throwing them something buoyant. The storm’s track and the warnings remain under review.

Further areas of England, southern Scotland and Wales are under yellow warnings for wind and rain, with possible disruption to buildings and transport and some power cuts. The Met Office says wet and unsettled conditions are expected to continue beyond the storm’s passage.

content.headline: Covid inquiry findings prompt fresh anger from care-home families
content.shortHeadline: Care-home families describe lasting harm from Covid isolation
content.standfirst: Relatives say restrictions left loved ones lonely and cut off from family, after an inquiry found the care sector was treated as an afterthought. Their accounts underline the personal cost of pandemic policies.

image.caption: The Covid memorial wall in London.

sources.originalTitle: No surprise and lasting anger: families of people who died in care homes react to Covid inquiry report

segments.body: Families of care-home residents who died during the pandemic have described the isolation their relatives endured, after a new Covid inquiry report criticised the handling of the sector. The inquiry said hospital discharges without testing helped spread the virus and that blanket limits on visits caused profound emotional harm.

segments.title: Families recall the separation
segments.body: Relatives told the Guardian that residents were left alone in their rooms, sometimes unable to speak with family or see loved ones except through glass. Some say they had believed the restrictions were necessary to protect residents, but now feel anger and regret about the time and contact lost.

A former care worker described staff facing fear, bereavement and shortages of protective equipment while residents became ill. The inquiry’s findings have reinforced families’ criticisms of the response, though their experiences and the circumstances in individual homes varied.

content.headline: UK trial tests diabetes and ADHD drugs as possible Alzheimer’s treatments
content.shortHeadline: UK trial tests metformin and ADHD drug for Alzheimer’s
content.standfirst: A new study will test several treatments in parallel, beginning with two medicines already used for other conditions. Researchers hope the approach will speed up the search for treatments, but benefit has not yet been demonstrated.

image.caption: Angela Bucksey is the first participant to begin treatment in the AD-SMART trial.

sources.originalTitle: Diabetes and ADHD drugs to be tested on Alzheimer's patients in new study

segments.body: A UK clinical trial is testing whether metformin, used for type 2 diabetes, and atomoxetine, used for ADHD, can help people with mild to moderate Alzheimer’s. The trial will compare several treatments with a placebo group and can stop testing a drug that shows no benefit.

segments.title: Measuring everyday effects
segments.body: Researchers plan to recruit 1,200 people at more than 30 sites. They will assess thinking and the ability to carry out everyday activities, alongside regular health checks. The first drugs are expected to be evaluated in 2030, and other treatments may be added before then.

The medicines were selected by an international panel because they may help reduce brain inflammation, the study’s lead investigator said. That is a rationale for testing them, not evidence that they will treat Alzheimer’s. People with a confirmed diagnosis can register interest in taking part.

content.headline: Met police investigate rape allegation against former DUP leader Jeffrey Donald
content.shortHeadline: Police investigate rape allegation against former DUP leader
content.standfirst: The Met says it is investigating an allegation relating to 2016 in the Palace of Westminster. No arrests have been made, and the inquiry is at an early stage.

image.caption: Jeffrey Donaldson led the DUP from 2021 to 2024.

sources.originalTitle: Jeffrey Donaldson investigated over alleged rape in UK parliament

segments.body: The Metropolitan police are investigating an allegation that former Democratic Unionist party leader Jeffrey Donaldson raped a woman inside the Palace of Westminster in 2016. The report was referred to the Met by Northern Ireland’s police service on 13 October.

The Met says the investigation is in its early stages, that no arrests have been made and that inquiries are continuing. The woman is being supported by specialist officers. Donaldson led the DUP from 2021 to 2024.

content.headline: Fridge recycling failures leave thousands of appliances piled up across UK
content.shortHeadline: Fridge recycling capacity fails as appliances pile up across the UK
content.standfirst: A shortage of specialist processing plants has left councils storing discarded fridges and freezers, with 26 authorities forced to stop accepting them this summer. The appliances can contain gases and materials that require careful handling.

image.caption: More than 3,000 fridges and freezers are stored at a former recycling centre in Norfolk.

sources.originalTitle: What an eyesore! My day at Norfolk’s frightful fridge mountain

segments.body: Thousands of unwanted fridges and freezers are being stored in piles across the UK as recycling capacity falls short. Norfolk has more than 3,000 at one site, while 26 local authorities stopped accepting the appliances this summer, according to reporting by the Guardian.

segments.title: Specialist plants are closing
segments.body: Fridges must be dismantled at specialist facilities because their refrigerants and insulation materials can harm the environment if handled improperly. Fires and closures have reduced the number of UK processing plants, while hot weather and older appliances have added to the pressure on councils.

Councils say the storage and collection burden is diverting public money, and warn that halted services may encourage fly-tipping. The government says it is working with local authorities and industry on temporary storage and longer-term solutions; Norfolk officials say their full site may remain occupied for some time.

content.headline: Danish emergency coordination team activated after global PHP security flaw
content.shortHeadline: Denmark activates low-level crisis response after PHP security flaw
content.standfirst: The National Operational Staff has been activated at its lowest readiness level after vulnerabilities in PHP disrupted online services. Authorities say they know of no websites hacked because of the flaw.

sources.originalTitle: Efter global sikkerhedsbrist aktiveres national krisestab
Dansk Industri advarer om alvorlige sikkerhedshuller på hjemmesider
Aula midlertidigt lukket efter mulig sikkerhedsrisiko
DMI's hjemmeside er ude af drift

segments.body: Denmark’s National Operational Staff has been activated at its lowest level, an information alert, after two serious vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP, software used to build many websites. The Ministry of Resilience and Preparedness confirmed the activation to DR.

segments.title: Services taken offline
segments.body: The municipal IT association Kombit confirmed that the PHP vulnerabilities were behind the closure of Aula, the communications platform used by schools and childcare services. DR also reported that the Danish Meteorological Institute and some municipal digital services had been taken offline or disrupted.

Authorities said they were not aware of any websites hacked because of the flaw. The emergency staff’s lowest-level activation involves closer monitoring and stronger communication between authorities; it does not necessarily require members to meet in person. Officials and industry groups urged organisations using PHP to apply the available updates immediately.

content.headline: Two men arrested after bus driver assaulted near Randers
content.shortHeadline: Two arrested after assault on bus driver near Randers
content.standfirst: Police say two passengers hit and kicked the driver after he challenged their behaviour and asked them to leave the bus. They are suspected of assaulting a public-service employee.

sources.originalTitle: To mænd anholdt efter overfald på buschauffør

segments.body: Two men have been arrested after a bus driver was assaulted in Hald, north of Randers, East Jutland Police said. The driver told the passengers to leave after challenging their behaviour; police say the two men then hit and kicked him.

The men, who police say were heavily intoxicated when the driver picked them up in Randers, were arrested nearby. They are charged with violence against a person performing a public service. The driver called emergency services.

content.headline: Como thrash Manchester United as Fernandes turns on Carrick over tactics
content.shortHeadline: Como thrash United as Fernandes criticises Carrick
content.standfirst: United’s 4-1 Champions League defeat extended their winless run to seven games. Captain Bruno Fernandes criticised the tactics, while Michael Carrick said the team’s failure to run was also to blame.

image.caption: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick acknowledges supporters after the 4-1 defeat by Como.

sources.originalTitle: Fernandes rounds on Carrick after Man Utd humiliation
Paz, Fabregas and Como teach Man Utd a lesson

segments.body: Manchester United were beaten 4-1 by Como, whose Nico Paz scored twice and set up another goal. United are now winless in seven games in all competitions, their longest such run since 2015, and are 13th in the Premier League.

segments.title: Blame and pressure
segments.body: Fernandes said United had given Como too much space and should sometimes have pressed higher. Asked whether Carrick got the tactics wrong, he replied: “That’s on the manager and staff to see it, not me.” Carrick, who apologised to supporters, responded that “if you don’t run forward, and you don’t run back, you aren’t going to win”.

segments.title: Como’s rise
segments.body: The result capped a remarkable rise for Como, who were in Italy’s fourth tier in 2017 and have reached the Champions League under coach Cesc Fabregas. Their chief executive said the club’s owners first became interested when Como were an amateur side; the club now faces scrutiny over how it will meet Uefa financial rules.

content.headline: Australia on the brink after being bowled out for 99 against South Africa
content.shortHeadline: Australia face Test defeat after collapse for 99
content.standfirst: South Africa have a strong chance to level the series after Australia’s batting collapsed on day four. The tourists remain behind in their second innings with a day left, but the match is not yet decided.

image.caption: Australia were 156-4 in their second innings after being bowled out for 99.

sources.originalTitle: 'Playing for their careers' - Australia reeling after extraordinary day

segments.body: Australia were bowled out for 99 in their first innings in Gqeberha, giving South Africa a substantial lead in the second Test. By the close of day four, Australia were 156-4 in their second innings, still 170 runs behind, with Travis Head unbeaten on 87.

segments.title: Questions over the batting
segments.body: Former Australia opener Simon Katich said players were “playing for their careers”. Coach Andrew McDonald criticised Marnus Labuschagne’s dismissal after he made 39, while acknowledging that South Africa had exposed weaknesses in the batting. Kagiso Rabada and Marco Jansen led the attack; Jansen took five wickets in the first innings.

Australia still have a chance to fight on: Head remains at the crease and McDonald said Steve Smith would bat on day five despite a neck issue. South Africa need six more wickets to finish the match and level the series; the outcome is not yet known.

content.headline: Saka injury worries Arsenal after early exit against Bayern
content.shortHeadline: Arsenal wait for news after Saka injury
content.standfirst: Bukayo Saka came off after 10 minutes of Arsenal’s 2-2 Champions League draw with Bayern Munich. Mikel Arteta said the sharp pain in the winger’s quadriceps was concerning, but no diagnosis or recovery timeline has been given.

image.caption: Bukayo Saka was withdrawn after 10 minutes with a quadriceps injury.

sources.originalTitle: Saka injury 'does not look good' - how will Arsenal cope?

segments.body: Saka went down without an opponent nearby and was replaced by Eberechi Eze. Arteta said those around the player were “a bit concerned” and that a player leaving the pitch with sharp pain was “never good news”. Arsenal are waiting to establish the extent of the injury.

segments.title: Options in attack
segments.body: Eze scored Arsenal’s opening goal, while Noni Madueke switched wings after Saka went off. Arteta praised the substitutes’ contribution. The report notes that Arsenal have other wide options, but Saka’s importance means his possible absence remains a concern.

content.headline: Kane strengthens Ballon d’Or case with goal and assist against Arsenal
content.shortHeadline: Kane’s Bayern display fuels Ballon d’Or case
content.standfirst: Harry Kane scored from the penalty spot and assisted Bayern’s other goal in their 2-2 draw with Arsenal. Declan Rice backed his England team-mate for the award, whose winner is due to be announced on Monday.

image.caption: Harry Kane’s performance against Arsenal added to the discussion around his Ballon d’Or chances.

sources.originalTitle: Goal, assist... goal-kick - Kane underlines Ballon d'Or credentials

segments.body: Kane helped Bayern equalise with a pass for Alphonso Davies, then put them ahead from the penalty spot before Rice’s late goal earned Arsenal a draw. Kane has scored 156 goals in 158 appearances for Bayern since joining in 2023.

segments.title: An unusual role
segments.body: Kane also took a Bayern goal-kick during the match and sent an 80-yard pass forward. BBC Sport pundit Nedum Onuoha said the moment reflected the freedom Kane has under Vincent Kompany to roam and create, as well as his willingness to work defensively.

perspectives.body: Onuoha said Kane’s freedom in Bayern’s system lets him create from varied positions, and that team-mates trust his decisions. He described the goal-kick as unusual for a number nine, but a moment that nearly created a goal.

segments.body: Rice called Kane “the clear winner” for the 2026 Ballon d’Or, citing his year and his quality as both a team-mate and opponent. Kane is on the 30-player shortlist; the winner will be announced in London on Monday. Kane said the voting had already closed and he would wait to see the result.

content.headline: Mark Allen says he spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic
content.shortHeadline: Allen reveals mental health treatment before return
content.standfirst: The former world number one says he is continuing treatment after spending 10 weeks in a mental health clinic. He returned to snooker this week following five months away and lost to Jordan Brown.

image.caption: Mark Allen returned to snooker after a five-month absence.

sources.originalTitle: Allen reveals mental health clinic stay before return

segments.body: Allen said in a statement that he discharged himself from a mental health clinic to prepare for Tuesday’s Northern Ireland Open match against friend Jordan Brown. He plans to continue treatment and said he is “doing my best to turn things round”.

segments.title: A return in progress
segments.body: Allen, 40, said he had been in a “bad place” and that the match might have been his last if he had not been drawn against Brown. He thanked his family, therapists, fellow patients and the World Snooker Tour for their support, and described himself as “a work in progress”.

content.headline: Lancashire do not offer James Anderson a new contract
content.shortHeadline: Anderson left without a new Lancashire deal
content.standfirst: The 44-year-old England great took 50 County Championship wickets this season, but Lancashire will not offer him a contract for 2027. Whether he retires or seeks another county is not known.

image.caption: James Anderson is England’s all-time leading Test wicket-taker, with 704 dismissals.

sources.originalTitle: Anderson, 44, not offered new Lancashire contract

segments.body: Lancashire have decided against offering Anderson a new deal, ending his time at the county unless he finds another playing option. He took 50 Championship wickets in 2026, the seventh-highest total in Division Two, and was named the county’s Championship player of the year.

segments.title: A remarkable record
segments.body: Anderson took 704 Test wickets for England, a record for a pace bowler, and 991 international wickets across formats. He played his final Test in 2024 after being asked to retire from international cricket. Lancashire have not commented, and it is not known whether he will retire or join another county.

content.headline: Kvaratskhelia to have surgery after rupturing ACL in PSG win
content.shortHeadline: Kvaratskhelia faces surgery for ruptured ACL
content.standfirst: Paris St-Germain have confirmed Khvicha Kvaratskhelia will have surgery after rupturing his anterior cruciate ligament against Barcelona. The club has not said how long the winger will be out.

image.caption: Khvicha Kvaratskhelia was making his first Champions League start of the season.

sources.originalTitle: PSG's Kvaratskhelia to have surgery on ruptured ACL

segments.body: Kvaratskhelia injured his right knee in a challenge during PSG’s 4-2 Champions League win over Barcelona and left the pitch in the 59th minute unable to put weight on his leg. PSG confirmed the ACL rupture and said he would undergo surgery, but gave no return timeline.

The Georgia international said he had prepared especially hard for the match and would work through “months of hard work, pain, tears” before trying to return. PSG also confirmed that Ousmane Dembele and Marquinhos would be absent for “a few weeks” with thigh injuries.

content.headline: Hyron Andrews died of natural causes after a tear in a heart artery
content.shortHeadline: Autopsy finds former Sale player Andrews died naturally
content.standfirst: An autopsy found that former Sale second row Hyron Andrews died after a tear in his aorta. The 31-year-old was found at the hotel of his new team, the Lions, before their Champions Cup match in France.

image.caption: Hyron Andrews joined Sale midway through the 2023-24 season.

sources.originalTitle: Andrews died of tear in artery around heart - autopsy

segments.body: Andrews died of natural causes after a tear in the aorta caused blood to fill the sac around his heart, according to an autopsy. The 31-year-old had joined Johannesburg-based Lions this summer and was found unconscious in a shower at the team hotel before their match against La Rochelle.

segments.title: Tributes
segments.body: Andrews’ wife, Maighlin, asked for “respect, privacy and patience” as the process of returning his body to South Africa begins. The Lions played in his honour, and former club Sale also paid tribute; director of rugby Alex Sanderson said the team loved playing and spending time with him.

content.headline: Kiran Leonard finds a path beyond the teenage-prodigy label
content.shortHeadline: Kiran Leonard moves beyond the prodigy years
content.standfirst: Once patronised for his precocious, densely composed music, the Saddleworth-born artist describes leaving his first industry team and finding a new creative community in London.

image.caption: Kiran Leonard, experimental musician and songwriter.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I had no plan. Just total scorched earth’: how Kiran Leonard survived teen success to make songs of full-body joy

segments.body: Kiran Leonard was hailed as a prodigy at 16, but says early coverage fetishised the ambition and complexity of his music in ways that felt patronising. After releasing four albums, he ditched his management team without a plan and struggled to find gigs or a new manager.

segments.title: Finding a different voice
segments.body: Leonard gradually found his footing through shows and friendships with musicians including Caroline. He now sees his work as a series of distinct investigations, and says he is drawn less to stylistic labels than to sounds that create a physical feeling. Much of his work remains solitary, with collaborations offering a different voice.

content.headline: Brazilian pop fandoms mobilise online for Lula ahead of the runoff
content.shortHeadline: Brazilian pop fans campaign for Lula
content.standfirst: More than 600 fan groups have joined a digital campaign backing Brazil’s president in the 25 October runoff. Their organisers see fan communities as a way to bring political debate to people who may not follow it elsewhere.

image.caption: Two pop fans at a pro-Lula demonstration in São Paulo.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Taylor Swift tells us to take the lead!’ Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula?

segments.body: After the first round of Brazil’s presidential election, more than 600 fan groups for international and Brazilian pop artists joined Fandoms Pelo Brasil, an online campaign supporting Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. The runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro is scheduled for 25 October. The campaign grew from fan accounts offering Lula’s team access to their social media audiences.

perspectives.body: Organisers say fan accounts can carry political discussion to people who follow artists and fan communities but do not keep up with politics. The reporting also notes the limits: some Brazilian fan groups back Bolsonaro, while Shakira’s team has restricted political use of her image.

segments.title: Fandom becomes a campaign network
segments.body: The effort has moved from online posts to street organising, with pop-culture symbols appearing at a Lula rally in São Paulo. The government has also courted fans through measures such as a decree targeting ticket-scalping bots and requiring free drinking water at large public events. The groups’ support is not presented as universal, but their mobilisation has become part of the runoff campaign.

content.headline: Ed Sanders reflects on the Fugs and a life of countercultural protest
content.shortHeadline: Ed Sanders on the Fugs and a life of protest
content.standfirst: The 87-year-old musician, poet and activist speaks as a documentary about the Fugs reaches UK audiences, revisiting the band’s anti-war theatrics, battles over censorship and eclectic music.

image.caption: Ed Sanders, right, with Fugs bandmate Tuli Kupferberg.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We tried to levitate the Pentagon’: the almost unbelievable life of Ed Sanders, trickster god of the US counterculture

segments.body: Ed Sanders led the Fugs, whose mix of poetry, folk, garage rock and theatrical provocation made them part of New York’s 1960s counterculture. Speaking as the documentary Fugs Film! receives its UK premiere, Sanders recalls the band’s aim to protest the American war machine as well as make music.

perspectives.body: Sanders says the group’s plan to “levitate” the Pentagon was a deliberately absurd spectacle designed to focus attention on an anti-war protest. He describes that activism as a continuing struggle, not a victory secured in the 1960s.

segments.title: Art, provocation and the cost of refusing to compromise
segments.body: The band’s provocations brought censorship battles and, Sanders says, helped cost them an Atlantic Records release after he refused to remove an offensive song. He now sees some of the group’s songs differently, but argues that music and protest belonged together in the Fugs’ work.

content.headline: The Avalanches turn advertising jingles into a bittersweet sound collage
content.shortHeadline: The Avalanches make a collage of commercial noise
content.standfirst: No Bad Memories folds advertising voices and audio logos into the Australian group’s sample-rich pop. The review hears an exuberant, sprawling record shadowed by the fading shared references of mass media.

sources.originalTitle: No Bad Memories

segments.body: On No Bad Memories, the Avalanches build a continuous, 52-minute collage from decades of advertising jingles, audio logos and spoken copy, alongside vintage soul and easy listening. The interruption of a dance track by a flatly delivered “Toshiba” is both a joke and a reminder that the record’s playful sound is not outside commercial culture.

segments.title: A nostalgia without a monoculture
segments.body: The review finds the album closer to the immersive sample collage of Since I Left You than the group’s more conventional later songwriting, while noting its long track list and numerous interludes. Its deeper melancholy comes from the question of whether a sound can still summon collective nostalgia when audiences no longer share the same mass-media touchstones.

content.headline: Zach Bryan’s new EP finds focus in sobriety and a bid for adulthood
content.shortHeadline: Zach Bryan finds focus on a new EP
content.standfirst: On Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs, the country songwriter pares back his usual sprawl to examine sobriety, love and the damage of old habits. The review sees a more controlled, forward-looking record.

sources.originalTitle: Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs EP

segments.body: Young Manhood and Other Donatable Organs is Zach Bryan’s first music written and recorded while sober. Across eight songs, he looks back at personal turmoil and the habits he is trying to leave behind, in a more concise and controlled set than his often sprawling albums.

segments.title: The unevenness of moving on
segments.body: The review hears his strongest writing in songs about change, including a duet with Turnpike Troubadours singer Evan Felker that links shared roots to the difficult work of breaking harmful habits. A duet with Lana Del Rey is judged less successful, but the record’s overall movement from recent mistakes towards a possible future gives it its shape.

content.headline: Way Dynamic’s Massive Shoe finds tenderness in bruised pop songs
content.shortHeadline: Way Dynamic make warm pop with a bruised edge
content.standfirst: Dylan Young’s Melbourne group draws on familiar pop sounds for gentle melodies, but the album’s strongest moments turn on rambling guitars and sharply expressed regret.

sources.originalTitle: Massive Shoe

segments.body: Way Dynamic’s third album, Massive Shoe, moves between bright, guitar-led pop and looser, more searching songs. The review hears the record’s warmth in its stacked harmonies and melodic ease, but finds its most affecting work where that lightness meets the sting of a failed relationship.

segments.title: When the regret cuts through
segments.body: “Miffed It” is singled out for its plain admission of a love mishandled, while “I Was the Dancer” opens into an unexpectedly expansive, jam-like passage. Some of the album’s more playful references and arrangements are less substantial, but the review values the tension between Young’s sunny musical surfaces and unsettled lyrics.

content.headline: Renny Conti’s Split Second renders grief as a shifting haze
content.shortHeadline: Renny Conti writes through grief’s haze
content.standfirst: Written after the death of his older brother, Split Second moves between soft, drifting arrangements and moments of startling clarity. The review finds its most powerful passages when Conti’s memories become sharply specific.

sources.originalTitle: Split Second

segments.body: Renny Conti wrote Split Second in the months after his older brother Andrew died. Its quiet voice and slow-moving arrangements evoke grief as a disorienting presence: the knowledge that someone is gone colliding with the feeling that they remain close.

segments.title: Moments that come into focus
segments.body: The review praises the album’s hazy atmosphere but sometimes longs for more detail to break through it. A direct line placing Conti in Prospect Park as he writes to escape a “death-induced funk” provides that clarity; the album is most affecting, the critic argues, when its private loss takes vivid, particular form.

content.headline: Worldpeace DMT’s Stick Around for Tea turns indie pop into a playful musical
content.shortHeadline: Worldpeace DMT make a playful indie-pop musical
content.standfirst: The London duo’s digitally assembled songs sound like a deliberately scrappy stage show, balancing schoolyard playfulness with moments of genuine ache. The review finds the apparent silliness more carefully made than it first appears.

sources.originalTitle: Stick Around for Tea

segments.body: Worldpeace DMT’s Stick Around for Tea pares back the sound collage of the duo’s debut in favour of songs that feel like scenes in a low-budget musical. Chiptuned textures, toy-like sounds and singsong vocals keep the record playful, while Rowan Please’s performance and Leo Fincham’s arrangements reveal a deliberate tension between childhood and adulthood.

segments.title: A joke with feeling underneath
segments.body: The review points to “Stratocaster” as a sparse, darkly poetic song delivered with the simplicity of a nursery rhyme, and to the title track’s engineered contrast between synthetic rhythm and a human chorus. The record repeatedly invites the question of whether its creators are serious; the critic’s answer is that the self-conscious play is part of the craft, not evidence against it.

content.headline: Michael Jackson biopic sequel may address abuse allegations from his perspective
content.shortHeadline: Michael Jackson sequel may address abuse allegations
content.standfirst: Jaafar Jackson says a second film will offer more of his uncle’s point of view. That approach follows criticism that the authorised first biopic omitted allegations and the perspectives of those who made them.

image.caption: Jaafar Jackson as Michael Jackson in the film Michael.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s important that Michael’s voice is heard’: Jaafar Jackson says second biopic of his uncle will cover sexual abuse allegations

segments.body: Jaafar Jackson, who made his screen debut playing his uncle in Michael, says a second film will give more attention to the late singer’s perspective on the sexual abuse allegations against him. The first biopic did not address the allegations; a legal clause prevented the depiction of one accuser, and a planned police-raid sequence was cut.

segments.title: A disputed account
segments.body: Jackson says the family has wanted the singer’s voice heard. Dan Reed, director of the documentary Leaving Neverland, sharply criticised the first film for distorting the subject and excluding the allegations. Jackson was accused of sexually abusing a child in 1993 and settled out of court; he was acquitted of other child sexual abuse charges in 2005. How a sequel will handle the competing accounts remains unknown.

perspectives.body: Reed says the first biopic reversed the truth by presenting Jackson without serious scrutiny and objected to its omission of the allegations. Jaafar Jackson, by contrast, says a sequel should give greater weight to his uncle’s point of view.

content.headline: Ghosts cast explain why the finished sitcom is returning as a film
content.shortHeadline: Why the Ghosts team brought the story back as a film
content.standfirst: The creators say they had no plan to revive their sitcom after its 2023 finale. A new film gave them a way to reunite the ensemble without simply stretching a television episode to feature length.

image.caption: The Ghosts cast in Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We’ll keep doing this if people pay us!’ The cast of TV hit Ghosts on making a movie – and maybe a caveman spinoff

segments.body: Ghosts ended in 2023 with its creators believing the story was complete. The cast says a film only became appealing after they found a premise—possession—that could let one of the ghosts leave Button House and create stakes suited to a feature. The result, Ghosts: The Possession of Button House, continues the story without restarting the series.

segments.title: A reunion, not a promise of more
segments.body: The team describes the production as a quick decision driven partly by missing one another after years of working together. They are cautious about promising further films, though Laurence Rickard jokes that caveman Robin could support a spin-off. The creators say there is no secret project in development.

content.headline: Sitges festival finds horror in motherhood, politics and the uncanny
content.shortHeadline: The unsettling discoveries of the Sitges film festival
content.standfirst: This year’s fantastic film festival ranged from sinister children and body horror to an Indonesian prison ghost story. The critic’s highlights include films that mix genre shocks with social unease and unexpected warmth.

image.caption: A scene from The Spiral, one of the films screened at Sitges.

sources.originalTitle: Explosive births, talking foxes and the devil in a trenchcoat – the Sitges fantastic film festival in all its creepy glory

segments.body: The 59th Sitges festival was crowded with stories of fraught motherhood, from Nightborn’s unsettling newborn to films about postpartum depression and a child who disrupts a scout troop. Marion Le Coroller’s Sanguine won best feature, while the festival also recognised performances in The Spiral and The Birthday Party.

segments.title: Standout films beyond the competition
segments.body: The critic’s favourites included a time-loop story that darkens as it unfolds, a return to J-horror in The Mouths, and Sabu’s crime comedy Arrested Memory. The strongest recommendation is Joko Anwar’s Ghost in the Cell, which layers a supernatural curse onto prison violence and a critique of Indonesian corruption while retaining an unexpectedly warmhearted tone.

content.headline: Children of the Wicker Man turns a folk-horror legacy into family history
content.shortHeadline: The family story behind The Wicker Man
content.standfirst: Robin Hardy’s sons revisit the making and afterlife of his cult film, but the documentary’s personal force comes with gaps in the family account and unanswered questions about absent voices.

image.caption: A still from Children of the Wicker Man.

sources.originalTitle: Children of the Wicker Man review – how the folk-horror classic haunted the family that made it

segments.body: Children of the Wicker Man, made by Robin Hardy’s sons Justin and Dominic, connects the troubled production of the 1973 film with its rise from box-office failure to cult status. It also becomes a personal reckoning with a father who left one son’s life, making the documentary’s family history as prominent as the film’s legacy.

segments.title: The silences in the account
segments.body: The review admires the brothers’ willingness to share painful memories but finds the film weakened by missing perspectives, including those of their siblings and other people central to the story. Justin’s anger and Dominic’s greater sympathy give the documentary distinct emotional registers, but do not resolve the absences.

content.headline: Digger’s box-office failure sharpens its bleak climate-change warning
content.shortHeadline: Digger’s flop sharpens its climate warning
content.standfirst: Tom Cruise’s misanthropic satire has been pulled from many US cinemas after a disastrous opening. The film’s critic argues that its depiction of public complicity makes it a revealing, if deeply flawed, climate story.

image.caption: Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Cruise’s Digger is a commercial flop – but also the perfect climate film for our time

segments.body: In Digger, an oilman’s drilling triggers a vast iceberg that threatens Europe. The film has been savaged by critics and suffered a steep box-office drop; the article reports a predicted loss of $245m and says it was removed from more than 2,500 US theatres before its third week.

segments.title: A critique with its own blind spots
segments.body: The argument for the film is that it goes beyond blaming one oil executive, confronting viewers with their own dependence on fossil fuels and the reluctance to change. But the piece also notes its nihilism and its dismissal of clean energy, which undercuts the urgency of that critique. Its failure may also make studios less willing to back similarly direct climate films.

content.headline: Judi Dench calls Cats a waste of goodwill and talent
content.shortHeadline: Judi Dench reflects on the failed Cats film
content.standfirst: In a forthcoming memoir, Dench says the film’s intentions were honourable but its elements did not come together. She also describes discomfort on set and recalls the hostile response to the finished adaptation.

image.caption: Judi Dench as Old Deuteronomy in Cats.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Oh God, I can’t bear it’: Judi Dench says Cats film was ‘a waste of goodwill and talent’

segments.body: Judi Dench writes in her forthcoming memoir that the 2019 film adaptation of Cats was “a waste of all that goodwill and talent”. She says she never saw the final cut and cannot judge it herself, but understands why critics were hostile and felt ill at ease in her role as Old Deuteronomy.

segments.title: An unsuccessful production without villains
segments.body: Dench criticises how young dancers were left exhausted and ignored between takes, while also saying nobody set out to make a bad film and that the people involved had honourable intentions. Andrew Lloyd Webber has been much harsher, calling the adaptation wrong and saying the experience left him emotionally damaged.

perspectives.body: Dench describes a failed collaboration without assigning blame to individual makers. Lloyd Webber, who was not consulted in the way he expected, has repeatedly condemned the film and its treatment of the original musical.

content.headline: Hartlepool fishers turn suspected pollution into an environmental campaign
content.shortHeadline: Hartlepool fishers take their pollution concerns to film
content.standfirst: Jeanie Finlay’s documentary follows fishermen facing collapsing catches after a mass marine die-off. Their independent study finds evidence of a possible link to industrial chemicals, while officials have disputed their account.

image.caption: Hartlepool fisherman Stan Rennie in All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea.

sources.originalTitle: All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea review – stirring portrait of fishers driven to eco-activism

segments.body: After thousands of crabs, starfish and lobsters washed up dead on the northeast coast in 2021, Hartlepool fishermen suspected industrial pollution. An official investigation pointed instead to an algal bloom; unconvinced, the fishermen funded an independent study, which found evidence of a link to pyridine, a byproduct of steelmaking.

perspectives.body: The documentary follows the fishermen’s investigation and their belief that sediment dredged from the River Tees and dumped at sea may be responsible. The review reports evidence of a possible chemical link, not a settled finding of causation.

segments.title: Livelihoods and local power
segments.body: With catches down 80%, rising fuel costs and boats up for sale, the fishermen’s campaign is also a fight for their livelihoods. The film links the dispute to dredging for a Tees Valley freeport and shows the mayor dismissing the fishermen as conspiracy theorists and activists.

content.headline: Smart TVs leave some viewers worried about privacy and control
content.shortHeadline: Viewers push back against smart TV surveillance
content.standfirst: Some owners are disconnecting devices, modifying remotes or buying simpler screens to avoid unwanted updates, adverts and data collection. A report alleging LG TVs record audio has been denied by the company.

image.caption: A viewer with a smart television.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV

segments.body: Some viewers say smart TVs have become harder to use as software updates, paid-service prompts and advertising crowd out the simple functions they want. Several people interviewed keep their screens offline or use external devices, citing both reliability and privacy concerns.

perspectives.body: TV specialist Tom Parsons says cheaper sets can slow under the demands of their software, while noting that most shoppers still want an all-in-one entertainment system. That preference has left few straightforward, non-connected televisions on sale.

segments.title: The limits of opting out
segments.body: The article describes a YouTube investigation alleging that LG televisions record audio even when offline or powered down; LG denied the allegations. Some owners have responded by modifying devices, while proposed changes to broadcast services in the UK and Australia could make internet-connected viewing harder to avoid.

content.headline: Freddie Meredith goes from bar work to SNL UK in a rapid comedy ascent
content.shortHeadline: Freddie Meredith’s unlikely leap to SNL UK
content.standfirst: After waiting tables and reworking a struggling Edinburgh show, the comedian was asked to join Saturday Night Live UK at short notice. He discusses the awkward characters and observations that helped him find an audience.

image.caption: Comedian and SNL UK cast member Freddie Meredith.

sources.originalTitle: ‘They said: there’s this part … he’s an idiot!’ SNL UK’s Freddie Meredith on his unlikely route to comedy’s big leagues

segments.body: Freddie Meredith was working in a bar and preparing for his Edinburgh Fringe debut when his character show Need a Light? began to find an audience. A best newcomer nomination and a sold-out London transfer followed; just before the final Fringe performance, he was invited to join the cast of Saturday Night Live UK.

segments.title: The comedy of uncomfortable men
segments.body: Meredith’s work focuses on socially awkward men trying to fit in, drawing on jobs behind bars and small observations of people at the edge of a scene. He says his interest in men drawn to misogynistic online ideas is both comic material and a subject that needs careful handling: audiences may laugh without recognising the behaviour as troubling.

content.headline: Linda Cardellini embraces practical gore in Friday the 13th prequel
content.shortHeadline: Linda Cardellini enters the world of slasher horror
content.standfirst: In Crystal Lake, Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees, the original Friday the 13th killer. She describes the hands-on prosthetics behind the show’s bloodiest scenes and reflects on the long afterlife of Freaks and Geeks.

image.caption: Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees in Crystal Lake.

sources.originalTitle: ‘They pulled a guy’s face off. It’s my favourite bit!’ Linda Cardellini on Freaks and Geeks, Mad Men and slasher horror Crystal Lake

segments.body: Linda Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees in Crystal Lake, a prequel to the Friday the 13th films. She says one of the show’s most gruesome effects—a face pulled off with fishing wire—was created with practical prosthetics, and that seeing it happen helped shape her reaction.

segments.title: A career of unexpected turns
segments.body: Cardellini also looks back on Freaks and Geeks, cancelled before its first season had finished airing but later embraced as a lasting television favourite. After winning her first Emmy for DTF St Louis, she says she enjoys changing direction rather than committing to a “scream queen” identity.

content.headline: Aberfan survivors recall the long fight for justice in new documentary
content.shortHeadline: Aberfan’s families and their decades-long fight
content.standfirst: The documentary revisits the 1966 disaster and the failures that followed it, through the memories of survivors and bereaved families. Its review finds the treatment of the village by officials as distressing as the tragedy itself.

image.caption: The aftermath of the Aberfan disaster in 1966.

sources.originalTitle: Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back review – the contempt they have faced to get justice is sickening

segments.body: On 21 October 1966, a spoil tip engulfed a school and homes in Aberfan, killing 116 children and 28 adults. Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back begins with survivors’ and families’ memories before tracing the campaign to hold the National Coal Board and government to account.

segments.title: A second injury
segments.body: The documentary recounts how the inquiry blamed the Coal Board, yet no one was personally punished. Families also faced years of resistance over liability and the removal of the tips; the board demanded money from the disaster fund to pay for the work. The review highlights the village’s organising and the later return of the fund money by the Blair government.

content.headline: Seven shows to stream this week, from The Audacity to Lupin
content.shortHeadline: Seven shows to stream this week
content.standfirst: A new comedy about wealthy tech executives leads this week’s picks, alongside a killer-gnome series, a grooming documentary and new seasons of familiar streaming favourites.

image.caption: Billy Magnussen and Sarah Goldberg in The Audacity.

sources.originalTitle: The Audacity to Nobody Wants This: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Audacity, from Succession writer Jonathan Glatzer, sends up a rich, morally compromised tech CEO and the world around him. The guide says the comedy does not quite reach Succession’s heights, but finds plenty of bite in its portrait of people insulated by wealth.

segments.title: Other picks this week
segments.body: The week’s recommendations range from Australian horror-comedy Gnomes and a documentary about the online grooming and murder of Breck Bednar to returning series Nobody Wants This and Lupin. The selection also includes a Halloween edition of Last One Laughing and a three-part investigation into police access to the encrypted Sky ECC app.

content.headline: Tonight on TV: a ketamine documentary and rare Only Fools and Horses clips
content.shortHeadline: Tonight: ketamine, Only Fools and more
content.standfirst: Stacey Dooley meets long-term ketamine users, while Only Fools and Horses fans get a look at deleted scenes. The evening’s other picks include a family documentary and a Bafta-nominated film about addiction.

image.caption: Stacey Dooley in Down the K-Hole.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: Stacey Dooley learns about ‘ket bladder’

segments.body: Down the K-Hole follows Stacey Dooley as she speaks with long-term ketamine users about the effects of the drug, including bladder damage and the appeal of dissociation. The programme is presented as an eye-opening account of consequences, not as a first-hand investigation by Dooley into her own use.

segments.title: Other evening choices
segments.body: The schedule also offers previously unseen Only Fools and Horses clips, a documentary about a mother and daughter navigating addiction and estrangement, and a programme about novelist John le Carré. The guide rounds out its picks with baking, police drama and live sport.

content.headline: Time’s young offender institute drama shows how anger is reinforced
content.shortHeadline: Time examines anger inside a young offenders’ institute
content.standfirst: The third series of Jimmy McGovern’s prison drama follows boys held in near-isolation and the adults responsible for them. Its review finds a devastating account of violence, emotional need and a system that leaves little room for change.

image.caption: David Tennant and Louis McCartney in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time review – David Tennant’s furious drama is as important as Adolescence

segments.body: The final series of Time moves into a young offender institution where boys can be locked in their cells for 23 hours a day under a “keep apart” system. David Tennant plays a weary but not entirely unfeeling officer; Siobhan Finneran returns as a chaplain who has lost her faith but continues to work with the inmates.

perspectives.body: The review argues the series should receive the national attention given to Adolescence, while acknowledging that the prison system’s complexity and the bleakness of its subject may make that harder.

segments.title: What the drama makes visible
segments.body: The boys’ histories include serious violence, but the series also shows grief, abuse and a lack of language for emotion feeding further harm. The review praises the young cast and argues that the drama’s account of isolation and pent-up anger makes the realities of young offender institutions difficult to ignore.

content.headline: Sarah Solemani’s The Party brings class, grief and ambition to television
content.shortHeadline: Sarah Solemani on class, grief and The Party
content.standfirst: The actor, writer and showrunner discusses adapting Elizabeth Day’s novel into a drama about a journalist and a Tory politician, and how personal loss and class have shaped her work.

image.caption: Actor, writer and showrunner Sarah Solemani.

sources.originalTitle: Sarah Solemani: ‘I performed at my mum’s hospice bed two weeks before she died’

segments.body: Sarah Solemani stars in and runs The Party, adapted from Elizabeth Day’s novel. The drama follows a working-class journalist and a Conservative politician whose old friendship hides a secret. Solemani says she has long tried to bring stories about the British class system to television without being forced to treat class as a genre in itself.

segments.title: Writing from experience
segments.body: Solemani speaks about losing her mother at 16, the urgency that followed, and her view that creativity requires a willingness to be emotionally exposed. She also says the #MeToo movement changed working conditions on sets, describing a marked difference from her experience as a young actor.

content.headline: Penguin Colony turns an Antarctic expedition into a strange, critical odyssey
content.shortHeadline: Penguin Colony is a strange Antarctic odyssey
content.standfirst: This exploration game sends a penguin through a world of Nazis, Lovecraftian horrors and scattered words. Its fractured storytelling becomes a critique of the human urge to conquer and plunder.

image.caption: A penguin explores the Antarctic world of Penguin Colony.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: Penguin Colony casts the player as a penguin exploring an Antarctic landscape where Nazis pursue an ancient entity. Words replace the usual treasure as collectibles, and hopping between different penguin species changes how the player moves through the terrain.

segments.title: A history seen from another angle
segments.body: The review praises the game’s unsettling shifts between low-poly exploration, narrated expedition history and archive footage. Its eventual critique of Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi barbarism is tied to a wider invitation to experience the world without treating it as something to conquer, though technical glitches occasionally interrupt the play.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time remake makes a classic feel new under the thumbs
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time gets a striking Switch 2 remake
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s remake updates movement, camera and sound for Switch 2 while preserving the game’s familiar world and puzzles. Link’s new look is divisive, but the preview finds a coherent reimagining in motion.

image.caption: Link in Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

segments.body: The Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time gives Link a sprint, manual jump, free-rotating camera and a streamlined inventory. Familiar dungeons and puzzles remain, but the upgraded controls make the 1998 game feel markedly different to play.

perspectives.body: The preview sees Link’s glossy, wide-eyed redesign as a point of debate, but suggests its doll-like look may reflect a Japanese puppet-theatre tradition rather than a simple pursuit of 4K detail.

segments.title: The challenge of revisiting a classic
segments.body: The remake’s enhanced environments and newly orchestrated soundtrack help refresh the familiar adventure, though the reviewer questions whether Hyrule Field can recreate the freedom players felt in 1998. The more traditional dungeon structure may itself be part of the appeal for returning fans.

content.headline: Could a new wave of independent arcades bring gaming back to the high street?
content.shortHeadline: Independent arcades could bring gaming back to the high street
content.standfirst: After years of sprawling games designed to occupy players indefinitely, interest is growing in shorter experiences and social play. The case for independent arcades is less about nostalgia than shared discovery.

image.caption: Players return to the social experience of arcade gaming.

sources.originalTitle: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth

segments.body: The article argues that publishers’ pursuit of “forever games” has helped renew interest in shorter, more focused experiences. New arcade-minded titles and specialist venues suggest a possible return to gaming spaces where players can try different games without committing all their time to one.

segments.title: A local place for players
segments.body: Rather than simply reproducing retro bars, the model proposed is closer to an independent bookshop or record store: a curated collection, knowledgeable staff and events that help build a community. Arcade specialist Will Freeman sees small venues opening on that basis, though he cautions that the current signs do not amount to a boom.

perspectives.body: Freeman says gaming bars and cafés show that out-of-home gaming can be sustainable, but describes independent arcades as a handful of emerging projects rather than a boom.

content.headline: A £350 GTA collector’s box reflects gaming’s growing price barrier
content.shortHeadline: The £350 GTA box reflects gaming’s rising costs
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI merchandise box does not include the game itself. The article sees its price as part of a wider shift that risks making console and PC gaming feel like a luxury hobby.

image.caption: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI collector’s box.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s £350 Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection contains merchandise but no copy or download code for the game. With the game priced separately at £70, buying both would cost £420.

segments.title: Who can afford to play?
segments.body: The writer argues that expensive collector’s editions fit a broader pattern of rising console and game prices, as publishers pursue a smaller group of high-spending customers. Mobile games remain widely accessible, but the console and PC experiences that form the article’s focus are increasingly difficult to access without substantial spending.

content.headline: Westminster Abbey’s Roman sarcophagus likely held an Anglo-Saxon abbot
content.shortHeadline: Roman coffin likely held a medieval abbot
content.standfirst: Radiocarbon dating places the skeleton found inside the reused coffin in the late 10th or early 11th century. An archaeologist believes it may be the remains of Ælfwig, an abbot of Westminster, though the identity is not certain.

image.caption: The sarcophagus on display in Westminster Abbey’s Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries.

sources.originalTitle: Mystery of Roman sarcophagus unearthed at Westminster Abbey solved at last, expert says

segments.body: A skeleton found inside a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey is likely to be that of a high-ranking medieval churchman, says the abbey’s consultant archaeologist, Warwick Rodwell. Radiocarbon dating places the bones in the late 10th or early 11th century, centuries after the coffin was made.

segments.title: A possible identity
segments.body: Rodwell says the coffin’s size and a cross carved into its lid point to an important ecclesiastic. He suggests Ælfwig, who died around 1020, is a likelier candidate than another abbot, Wulfnoth. The evidence narrows the possibilities but does not establish who the man was.

content.headline: Australia’s first national count finds more than 1.19 million mice used in
content.shortHeadline: Australia counts mice and rats used in research
content.standfirst: A pilot study estimates that more than 1.19 million mice and nearly 47,000 rats were used in Australian research, teaching and testing in 2024. Researchers and animal-welfare advocates say public data can support transparency, policy and rehoming.

image.caption: Bella Lear of Understanding Animal Research Oceania, which supports publishing national animal-use data.

sources.originalTitle: More than a million mice used in Australian research annually, ‘overdue’ study finds

segments.body: Australia’s first nationwide count found 1,193,619 mice and 46,961 rats were used in research, teaching and testing in 2024, the most recent comparable year. The figure excludes animals bred for research but not used. The veterinarian who compiled the pilot study calls it a first step towards national statistics covering more species.

segments.title: Why publish the figures?
segments.body: The report’s advocates say consistent public statistics could help inform animal-welfare policy and build trust. An Australian RSPCA representative notes that research practices can affect animals’ welfare; a small-animal adoption organisation says a count could also help it assess how many animals might be suitable for rehoming.

content.headline: Seeing others break rules can fuel bigger violations, study finds
content.shortHeadline: Others’ rule-breaking can encourage bigger violations
content.standfirst: In an online experiment with 750 US participants, observing someone flout a rule more brazenly led some people to break it further themselves. The researchers say the abstract task cannot show how reliably the effect translates to real life.

sources.originalTitle: Bad apple effect: study shows how people are influenced by rule-breaking of others

segments.body: Researchers asked 750 people in the US to complete a task in which rule-breaking could earn a larger reward. Participants saw how much another person had bent the rules and could then change their own choices. Observing rule-following slightly reduced violations; seeing small violations slightly increased them.

segments.title: The limits of the experiment
segments.body: The strongest increase followed examples of more flagrant rule-breaking: some participants exceeded the violations they had seen. The effect was stronger when participants shared the other person’s political leaning. The researchers’ simulations suggest escalation could spread, but an outside expert cautions that the abstract task had no penalty and does not establish how the pattern works in real-world settings.

content.headline: Optogenetics moves from algae research towards experimental treatments
content.shortHeadline: Light-controlled nerve cells move towards treatments
content.standfirst: A light-sensitive protein from a single-celled alga lets researchers control nerve cells with light. Early work includes a small trial that improved some severely impaired patients’ vision, while possible applications for pain, epilepsy and hearing remain at different stages of development.

image.caption: The single-celled alga Chlamydomonas, whose light-sensing protein helped enable optogenetics.

sources.originalTitle: The humble one-celled alga that helped scientists win the Nobel prize
A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: Optogenetics began with a discovery about Chlamydomonas, a single-celled alga that uses a light-sensing protein to trigger electrical signals. Researchers transferred the gene for that protein into animal nerve cells, creating a precise way to switch cells on or off with light. The method has helped scientists investigate brain circuits and behaviour.

segments.title: Clinical work is still early
